<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
    // Pre-apply spinout-banner dismissal here, before the banner paints, so it
    // never flashes in only to be hidden later by the deferred arxiv-header.js.
    // Key matches arxiv-header.js: "arxiv-banner-dismissed:" + data-banner-name.
    if (localStorage.getItem('arxiv-banner-dismissed:spinout-nonprofit')) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-banner-dismissed", "");
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Although deep models have been widely explored in solving partial differential equations (PDEs), previous works are primarily limited to data only with up to tens of thousands of mesh points, far from the million-point scale required by industrial simulations that involve complex geometries. In the spirit of advancing neural PDE solvers to real industrial applications, we present Transolver++, a highly parallel and efficient neural solver that can accurately solve PDEs on million-scale geometries. Building upon previous advancements in solving PDEs by learning physical states via Transolver, Transolver++ is further equipped with an extremely optimized parallelism framework and a local adaptive mechanism to efficiently capture eidetic physical states from massive mesh points, successfully tackling the thorny challenges in computation and physics learning when scaling up input mesh size. Transolver++ increases the single-GPU input capacity to million-scale points for the first time and is capable of continuously scaling input size in linear complexity by increasing GPUs. Experimentally, Transolver++ yields 13% relative promotion across six standard PDE benchmarks and achieves over 20% performance gain in million-scale high-fidelity industrial simulations, whose sizes are 100<math id="abstract1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> larger than previous benchmarks, covering car and 3D aircraft designs.</p>
  
</div>
<div class="ltx_keywords">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_keywords">Keywords: </h6>Machine Learning, ICML
</div><span id="id1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_affiliationnotice"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">†</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">†</sup><span class="ltx_note_type">affiliationnotice: </span>Equal contribution</span></span></span>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Extensive physics processes can be precisely described by partial differential equations (PDEs) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wazwaz, 2002</a>; <a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Evans, 2010</a>)</cite>, such as air dynamics of driving cars or internal stress of buildings. Accurately solving these PDEs is essential to industrial manufacturing <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kopriva, 2009</a>; <a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Roubíček, 2013</a>)</cite>. However, it is hard and usually impossible to obtain the analytic solution of PDEs. Thus, numerical methods <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ŝolín, 2005</a>)</cite> have been widely explored, whose typical solving process is first discretizing PDEs into computation meshes and then approximating solution on discretized meshes <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Grossmann et al., 2007</a>)</cite>. In real applications, such as simulating a driving car or aircraft during takeoff, it will take several days or even months for calculation, and the simulation accuracy is highly affected by the fitness of discretized computation mesh <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">Solanki et al., 2003</a>; <a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Elrefaie et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. To speed up this process, deep models have been explored as efficient surrogates of numerical methods, known as neural PDE solvers <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2023</a>)</cite>. Training from pre-collected simulation data, neural solvers can learn to approximate the mapping between input and output of numerical methods and directly infer new samples in a flash <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2021</a>)</cite>, posing a promising direction for industrial simulation.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Usually, industrial applications involve large and complex geometries, requiring the model to capture intricate physics processes underlying geometries efficiently. Although previous works have made some progress in handling complex geometries <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2023b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hao et al., 2023</a>)</cite> and attempted to speed up model efficiency, they are still far from real applications, especially in handling large geometries. Specifically, as illustrated in Figure <a href="#S1.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Transolver++: An Accurate Neural Solver for PDEs on Million-Scale Geometries" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>(a), existing models fail to scale up beyond 400k points, while real applications typically involves million-scale mesh points or even more. Note that, as aforementioned, the fineness of computation meshes is the foundation of simulation accuracy. As the comparison of car mesh shown in Figure <a href="#S1.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Transolver++: An Accurate Neural Solver for PDEs on Million-Scale Geometries" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>(b), limited mesh size will seriously sacrifice the precision of the geometry, where the originally streamlined surface becomes rough and uneven. This will further limit the simulation accuracy of physics processes, especially for aerodynamic applications <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Elrefaie et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. Thus, <em id="S1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">the capability of handling large geometries is indispensable for practical neural PDE solvers.</em></p>
</div>
<figure id="S1.F1" class="ltx_figure">
<p id="S1.F1.2" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center ltx_align_center"><span id="S1.F1.2.1" class="ltx_text"><img src="2502.02414v1/gpu_memory_short.png" id="S1.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/119;" width="476" height="119" alt="Refer to caption"></span></p>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 1: </span>(a) Comparison of model capability in handling large geometries. We plot the GPU memory change of each model when increasing input mesh points. The upper bound on a single A100 40GB GPU is depicted in the dotted line. (b) Comparison of experiment benchmarks. Transolver++ experiments on high-fidelity tasks with up to 2.5 million points, which is 100<math id="S1.F1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> larger than previous works.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">As the latest progress in neural PDE solver architectures, Transolver <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wu et al., 2024</a>)</cite> proposes to learn intrinsic physical states underlying complex geometries and apply the attention mechanism among learned physical states to capture intricate physics interactions, which frees model capacities from unwieldy mesh points and achieves outstanding performance in car and airfoil simulations. Although Transolver demonstrates favorable capability in handling complex geometries, its maximum input size remains limited to 700k points (Figure <a href="#S1.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Transolver++: An Accurate Neural Solver for PDEs on Million-Scale Geometries" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>(a)), and its experiment data is much simpler than real applications. Building on the essential step made by Transolver, we attempt to advance it to million-scale or even larger geometries in pursuing practical neural solvers.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">When scaling Transolver to million-scale high-fidelity PDE-solving tasks, we observe its bottlenecks in physics learning and computation efficiency. Firstly, as Transolver highly relies on the learned physical states, massive mesh points may overwhelm their learning process, resulting in homogeneous physical states and model degeneration. Secondly, it is observed that even deep representations of million-scale points without considering intermediate calculations will consume considerable GPU memory, which is strictly constrained by total resources on a single GPU. This drives us to elaboratively optimize the model architecture and unlock the power of multi-GPU parallelism. Thus, in this paper, we present <em id="S1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Transolver++</em>, which upgrades Transolver with an extremely optimized parallelism framework and a local adaptive mechanism to efficiently capture eidetic physical states from massive mesh points. Based on the co-design with model architecture, our parallelism framework significantly reduces the communication overhead and achieves linear scalability with resources without sacrificing performance. As a result, Transolver++ achieves consistent state-of-the-art on six standard PDE datasets and successfully extends Transolver to high-fidelity car and aircraft simulation tasks with million-scale points. Here are our contributions:</p>
<ul id="S1.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To ensure reliable modeling for complex physical interactions, we introduce Transolver++ with eidetic states, which can adaptively aggregate information from massive mesh points to distinguishable physical states.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We present an efficient and highly parallel implementation of Transolver++ with linear scalability and minimal overhead across GPUs, affording mesh size of 1.2 million on a single GPU while maintaining accuracy.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Transolver++ achieves a 13% relative gain averaged from six standard benchmarks and over 20% improvement on high-fidelity million-scale industrial datasets, covering practical car and 3D aircraft design tasks.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Related Work</h2>

<section id="S2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.1 </span>Neural PDE Solver</h3>

<div id="S2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Traditional numerical methods for solving PDEs often require high computational costs to achieve accurate solutions <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">Solanki et al., 2003</a>)</cite>. Recently, deep learning methods have demonstrated remarkable potential as efficient surrogate models for solving PDEs due to their inherent non-linear modeling capability, known as neural PDE solvers.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">As a typical paradigm, operator learning has been widely studied for solving PDEs by learning the mapping between input functions and solutions. FNO <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2020a</a>)</cite> first proposes to approximate integral in the Fourier domain for PDE solving. Subsequently, Geo-FNO <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2021</a>)</cite> extends FNO to irregular meshes by transforming them into regular grids in the latent space. To further enhance the capabilities of FNO, U-FNO <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wen et al. (2022)</a></cite> and U-NO <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Rahman et al. (2023)</a></cite> are presented by leveraging U-Net <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ronneberger et al., 2015</a>)</cite> to capture multiscale properties. Considering the high dimensionality of real-world PDEs, LSM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wu et al., 2023</a>)</cite> applies spectral methods in a learned lower-dimensional latent space to approximate input-output mappings. Afterward, LNO <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang &amp; Wang, 2024</a>)</cite> adopts the attention mechanism to effectively map data from geometric space to latent space for complex geometries.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Recently, Transformers <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">Vaswani et al., 2017</a>)</cite> have achieved impressive progress in extensive fields and have also been applied to solving PDEs, where the attention mechanism has been proven as a Monte-Carlo approximation for global integral <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kovachki et al., 2023</a>)</cite>. However, standard attention suffers from quadratic complexity. Thus, many models like Galerkin <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cao, 2021</a>)</cite>, OFormer <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2023c</a>)</cite> and FactFormer <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tran et al., 2023</a>)</cite> propose different efficient attention mechanisms. Among them, GNOT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hao et al., 2023</a>)</cite> utilizes well-established linear attention, like Reformer or Performer <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kitaev et al., 2020</a>; <a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Choromanski et al., 2021</a>)</cite>, and separately encodes geometric information, achieving favorable performance. However, linear attention often suffers from degraded performance as an approximation of standard attention <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qin et al., 2022</a>)</cite>. Moreover, these Transformer-based methods treat input geometries as a sequence of mesh points and directly apply attention among mesh points, which may fall short in geometric learning and computation efficiency. As a significant advancement in PDE solving, Transolver <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wu et al., 2024</a>)</cite> introduces the Physics-Attention mechanism that groups massive mesh points into multiple physical states and applies attention among states, thereby enabling more effective and intrinsic modeling of complex physical correlations. However, it still faces challenges in degenerated physics learning and a high computation burden under million-scale geometries. These challenges will be well addressed in our paper.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">In addition to Transformers, graph neural networks (GNNs) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hamilton et al., 2017</a>; <a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gao &amp; Ji, 2019</a>; <a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Pfaff et al., 2021</a>)</cite> are also inherently suitable to process unstructured meshes by explicitly modeling the message passing among nodes and edges. GNO <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2020b</a>)</cite> first implements neural operator with GNN.
Later, GINO <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2023a</a>)</cite> combines GNO with Geo-FNO to encode the geometry information. Recently, 3D-GeoCA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Deng et al., 2024</a>)</cite> integrates pre-trained 3D vision models to achieve a better representation learning of geometries. However, prone to geometric instability <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Klabunde &amp; Lemmerich, 2023</a>)</cite>, GNNs can lead to unstable results and may be insufficient in capturing global physics interactions, especially when handling large-scale unstructured meshes <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Morris et al., 2023</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.2 </span>Parallelism of Deep Models</h3>

<div id="S2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Despite processing large-scale geometries being crucial in industrial design, this problem has not been explored in previous research. This paper breaks the computation bottleneck by leveraging the parallelism framework, which is related to the following seminal works. Towards general needs in handling the high GPU memory usage caused by large-scale inputs, several parallel frameworks have been proposed, such as tensor parallelism <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shoeybi et al., 2019</a>)</cite> and model parallelism <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Huang et al., 2019</a>)</cite>. However, these methods are highly model-dependent and request significant communication overhead <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib53" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhuang et al., 2023</a>)</cite>. Another direction is to optimize attention mechanisms. Ring attention <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, inspired by FlashAttention <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dao et al., 2022</a>)</cite>, uses a ring topology between multi-GPUs, achieving quadratic communication complexity with respect to mesh points. Besides, DeepSpeed-Ulysses <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jacobs et al., 2023</a>)</cite> splits the deep representation along the channel dimension and employs the All2All communication approach, reducing complexity to linear. Despite these improvements, the communication volume remains excessive. In contrast, Transolver++ leverages its unique physics-learning design and presents a highly optimized parallelism framework tailored to PDE solving, enabling minimal communication overhead and allowing for meshes of million-scale points.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Revisiting Transolver</h2>

<figure id="S3.F2" class="ltx_figure">
<p id="S3.F2.2" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center ltx_align_center"><span id="S3.F2.2.1" class="ltx_text"><img src="2502.02414v1/eidetic_state.png" id="S3.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/119;" width="476" height="119" alt="Refer to caption"></span></p>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 2: </span>(a) Overall design of Transolver++ block. Blocks highlighted in red represent modifications compared to the original Transolver. (b) Visualization of slice weights. Transolver++ learns more diverse and eidetic physical states. (c) Visualizations of physical quantity change ratio (difference between each point and its neighbors) and slice weights learned by models. The lighter color means faster change.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Before Transolver++, we would like to briefly introduce Physics-Attention, the key design of Transolver <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wu et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, and discuss its scaling issues for million-scale inputs.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p2.2" class="ltx_p">Given meshes with <math id="S3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>N</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N</annotation></semantics></math> nodes, to capture intrinsic physics interactions under unwieldy mesh points, Physics-Attention will first assign <math id="S3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>C</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C</annotation></semantics></math>-channel input points <math id="S3.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{x}=\{\mathbf{x}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times C}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐱</mi><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>N</mi></msubsup><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{x}=\{\mathbf{x}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times C}</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="S3.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math> <em id="S3.p2.2.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">physical states</em> <math id="S3.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{s}=\{\mathbf{s}_{j}\}_{j=1}^{M}\in\mathbb{R}^{M\times C}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐬</mi><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>𝐬</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>M</mi></msubsup><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{s}=\{\mathbf{s}_{j}\}_{j=1}^{M}\in\mathbb{R}^{M\times C}</annotation></semantics></math> based on the slice weights <math id="S3.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{w}=\{\mathbf{w}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times M}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐰</mi><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>𝐰</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>N</mi></msubsup><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{w}=\{\mathbf{w}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times M}</annotation></semantics></math> learned from inputs, and each <math id="S3.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{w}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{1\times M}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐰</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{w}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{1\times M}</annotation></semantics></math> represents the possibility that <math id="S3.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{x}_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{x}_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> belongs to each state. Specifically, physical states are aggregated from all point representations based on learned slice weights, which can be formalized as:</p>
<table id="S3.E1" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_table">
<tbody>
<tr id="S3.E1X" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_eqn_cell"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E1X.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\text{Slice weights:}\ \mathbf{w}=\operatorname{Softmax}\left(\operatorname{Linear}(\mathbf{x})/\tau_{0}\right)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mtext>Slice weights:</mtext><mi>𝐰</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>Softmax</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>Linear</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐱</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>/</mo><mi>τ</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\text{Slice weights:}\ \mathbf{w}=\operatorname{Softmax}\left(\operatorname{Linear}(\mathbf{x})/\tau_{0}\right)</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>

<tr id="S3.E1Xa" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">

<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.p2.3" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.p2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>τ</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau_{0}</annotation></semantics></math> is the temperature constant. Next, the canonical attention mechanism is applied to learned physical states to capture underlying physics interactions:</p>
<table id="S3.E2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\begin{split}\mathbf{q},\mathbf{k},\mathbf{v}=\operatorname{Linear}(\mathbf{s}),\ \mathbf{s}^{\prime}=\operatorname{Softmax}\left(\frac{\mathbf{q}\mathbf{k}^{\top}}{\sqrt{C}}\right)\mathbf{v}.\end{split}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mtable displaystyle="true"><mtr><mtd class="ltx_align_right" columnalign="right"><mrow><mrow><mi>𝐪</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝐤</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>𝐯</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>Linear</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐬</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="1.167em">,</mo><mrow><msup><mi>𝐬</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>Softmax</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mfrac><msup><mi>𝐪𝐤</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msup><msqrt><mi>C</mi></msqrt></mfrac><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝐯</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\begin{split}\mathbf{q},\mathbf{k},\mathbf{v}=\operatorname{Linear}(\mathbf{s}),\ \mathbf{s}^{\prime}=\operatorname{Softmax}\left(\frac{\mathbf{q}\mathbf{k}^{\top}}{\sqrt{C}}\right)\mathbf{v}.\end{split}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(2)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.p2.4" class="ltx_p">Finally, Physics-Attention employs the <em id="S3.p2.4.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">deslice</em> operation to map updated states <math id="S3.p2.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{s}^{\prime}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>𝐬</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{s}^{\prime}</annotation></semantics></math> back to mesh space using slice weights, i.e. <math id="S3.p2.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{x}^{\prime}=\{\mathbf{x}_{i}^{\prime}\}_{i=1}^{N}=\{\sum_{j=1}^{M}\mathbf{w}_{ij}\mathbf{s}_{j}^{\prime}\}_{i=1}^{N}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>𝐱</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>i</mi><mo>′</mo></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>N</mi></msubsup><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><msubsup><mo lspace="0em">∑</mo><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>M</mi></msubsup><mrow><msub><mi>𝐰</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐬</mi><mi>j</mi><mo>′</mo></msubsup></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>N</mi></msubsup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{x}^{\prime}=\{\mathbf{x}_{i}^{\prime}\}_{i=1}^{N}=\{\sum_{j=1}^{M}\mathbf{w}_{ij}\mathbf{s}_{j}^{\prime}\}_{i=1}^{N}</annotation></semantics></math>. By replacing standard attention in Transformer <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">Vaswani et al., 2017</a>)</cite> with Physics-Attention, we can obtain the Transolver.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Although Transolver successfully reduces canonical computation complexity from <math id="S3.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{O}(N^{2})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>N</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{O}(N^{2})</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="S3.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{O}(M^{2})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>M</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{O}(M^{2})</annotation></semantics></math> by learning physical states (<math id="S3.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math> is a constant and usually set as 32 or 64 in practice), Transolver still face the following challenges when scaling input size to million-scale, i.e. <math id="S3.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N\geq 10^{6}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>≥</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mn>6</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N\geq 10^{6}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Homogeneous physical states</h5>

<div id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Eq. (<a href="#S3.E1" title="Equation 1 ‣ 3 Revisiting Transolver ‣ Transolver++: An Accurate Neural Solver for PDEs on Million-Scale Geometries" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>) shows that physical states are highly affected by slice weights <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{w}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐰</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{w}</annotation></semantics></math>. If <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{w}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐰</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{w}</annotation></semantics></math> tends to be uniform, attention in Eq. (<a href="#S3.E2" title="Equation 2 ‣ 3 Revisiting Transolver ‣ Transolver++: An Accurate Neural Solver for PDEs on Million-Scale Geometries" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>) will degenerate to average pooling, losing the physics modeling capability. As shown in Figure <a href="#S3.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 3 Revisiting Transolver ‣ Transolver++: An Accurate Neural Solver for PDEs on Million-Scale Geometries" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>(b), we find that Transolver may generate less distinguishable weights in some cases, especially in large-scale meshes, leading to homogeneous physical states.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Efficiency bottleneck</h5>

<div id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Although Physics-Attention cost is nearly constant when scaling the input, the feedforward layer to embed million-scale points by <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{x}_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{x}_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> will consume huge GPU memory, forming Transolver’s stability bottleneck.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Transolver++</h2>

<div id="S4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To tackle the scaling issues of Transolver in physics learning and computation efficiency, we present Transolver++, which can effectively avoid attention degeneration by learning eidetic physical states and successfully break the efficiency bottleneck with a highly optimized parallelism framework.</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1 </span>Physics-Attention with Eidetic States</h3>

<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">As aforementioned, if Physics-Attention is based on homogeneous physical states, it will degenerate to average pooling, which will damage the model’s performance. Thus, as the authors mentioned in Transolver <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wu et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, they adopt the softmax function in calculating slice weights in Eq. (<a href="#S3.E1" title="Equation 1 ‣ 3 Revisiting Transolver ‣ Transolver++: An Accurate Neural Solver for PDEs on Million-Scale Geometries" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>), which can alleviate the indistinguishable states to some extent by guaranteeing peakier distribution <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wu et al., 2022</a>)</cite>. However, we still observe the degeneration phenomenon when the model depth increases, as shown in Figure <a href="#S3.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 3 Revisiting Transolver ‣ Transolver++: An Accurate Neural Solver for PDEs on Million-Scale Geometries" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>(b), which may result from the excessive focus on global information. Note that in industrial applications, the model’s capability of learning subtle physics is essential, which may highly affect the evaluation in industrial design <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Elrefaie et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, as a small diversion device can drastically change the wind drag of driving cars.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To capture detailed physics phenomena, we propose to learn eidetic states by augmenting Transolver’s state learning with a local-adaptive mechanism and slice reparameterization to carefully control the learned slice weight distribution.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F3" class="ltx_figure">
<p id="S4.F3.2" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center ltx_align_center"><span id="S4.F3.2.1" class="ltx_text"><img src="2502.02414v1/distributed.png" id="S4.F3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/128;" width="476" height="128" alt="Refer to caption"></span></p>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 3: </span>(a) Comparison with other parallel methods. Tailored to the unique physics learning design, our method only communicates physical states with an all-reduce operation. (b) Scalability of the communication overhead to the number of mesh points with 32 GPUs. Our parallel method stands out by only transferring 0.25MB of data, which does not scale with the size of input mesh points. </figcaption>
</figure>
<section id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Local adaptive mechanism</h5>

<div id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">As shown in Figure <a href="#S3.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 3 Revisiting Transolver ‣ Transolver++: An Accurate Neural Solver for PDEs on Million-Scale Geometries" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>(b), modeling the distribution of each mesh point using a non-parametric approach has been proven to be impractical <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib52" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ye et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. Thus, we introduce a local adaptive mechanism that incorporates local information as a pointwise adjustment to the physics learning process. Specifically, we change the sharpness of the state distribution by learning to adjust the temperature <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>τ</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau_{0}</annotation></semantics></math> in the Softmax function, namely</p>
<table id="S4.E3" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E3.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\text{Ada-Temp:}\ \tau=\left\{\tau_{i}\right\}_{i=1}^{N}=\left\{\tau_{0}+\operatorname{Linear}(\mathbf{x}_{i})\right\}_{i=1}^{N}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mtext>Ada-Temp:</mtext><mi>τ</mi><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo>{</mo><msub><mi>τ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>N</mi></msubsup><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo>{</mo><msub><mi>τ</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><mi>Linear</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>N</mi></msubsup><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{Ada-Temp:}\ \tau=\left\{\tau_{i}\right\}_{i=1}^{N}=\left\{\tau_{0}+\operatorname{Linear}(\mathbf{x}_{i})\right\}_{i=1}^{N},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(3)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times 1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times 1}</annotation></semantics></math> and a higher temperature forms a more uniform distribution, while a lower temperature makes the distribution more concentrated on crucial states. Through a learnable linear projection layer, we can dynamically adjust the state distribution based on each point’s local properties.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Slice reparameterization</h5>

<div id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">As mentioned above, we try to learn eidetic physical states and assign mesh points to physical states with a possibility <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{w}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐰</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{w}</annotation></semantics></math>. In the canonical design of Transolver, it uses <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\operatorname{Softmax}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>Softmax</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\operatorname{Softmax}</annotation></semantics></math> to form a categorical distribution across states. However, simply generating a categorical distribution is not enough, as we have not completely modeled the assignment process from points to certain physical states. Considering that direct sampling via <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\operatorname{Argmax}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>Argmax</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\operatorname{Argmax}</annotation></semantics></math> is non-differentiable, we propose to adopt the Gumbel-Softmax <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jang et al., 2017</a>)</cite> to perform differentiable sampling from the discrete categorical distribution, which is accomplished with the following reparameterization technique:</p>
<table id="S4.E4" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{Rep-Slice}(\mathbf{x},{\mathbf{\tau}})=\operatorname{Softmax}\left(\frac{\operatorname{Linear}(\mathbf{x})-\log(-\log\mathbf{\epsilon})}{\tau}\right)," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mtext>Rep-Slice</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐱</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>τ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>Softmax</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mrow><mi>Linear</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐱</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mo rspace="0.167em">−</mo><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mi>ϵ</mi></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mi>τ</mi></mfrac><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{Rep-Slice}(\mathbf{x},{\mathbf{\tau}})=\operatorname{Softmax}\left(\frac{\operatorname{Linear}(\mathbf{x})-\log(-\log\mathbf{\epsilon})}{\tau}\right),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(4)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{\tau}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times 1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{\tau}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times 1}</annotation></semantics></math> is the local adaptive temperature and <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon=\{\epsilon_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N},\epsilon_{i}\sim\mathcal{U}(0,1)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>ϵ</mi><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>ϵ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>N</mi></msubsup></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>ϵ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒰</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon=\{\epsilon_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N},\epsilon_{i}\sim\mathcal{U}(0,1)</annotation></semantics></math>. Here <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\log(-\log\epsilon_{i})\sim\text{Gumbel}(0,1)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mo rspace="0.167em">−</mo><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><msub><mi>ϵ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mtext>Gumbel</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\log(-\log\epsilon_{i})\sim\text{Gumbel}(0,1)</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\operatorname{Gumbel}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>Gumbel</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\operatorname{Gumbel}</annotation></semantics></math> is a type of generalized extreme value distribution. Replacing Transolver’s slice weights <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{w}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐰</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{w}</annotation></semantics></math> in Eq. (<a href="#S3.E1" title="Equation 1 ‣ 3 Revisiting Transolver ‣ Transolver++: An Accurate Neural Solver for PDEs on Million-Scale Geometries" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>) by our new design in Eq. (<a href="#S4.E4" title="Equation 4 ‣ Slice reparameterization ‣ 4.1 Physics-Attention with Eidetic States ‣ 4 Transolver++ ‣ Transolver++: An Accurate Neural Solver for PDEs on Million-Scale Geometries" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>), Transolver++ is able to learn eidetic physical states under complex geometries, offering the possibility to handle much larger-scale datasets.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">As shown in Figure <a href="#S3.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 3 Revisiting Transolver ‣ Transolver++: An Accurate Neural Solver for PDEs on Million-Scale Geometries" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>(c), the slice weights in Transolver++ can perfectly adapt to the intricate physics fields on complex geometries. Specifically, regions with slow-changing physics quantities are assigned to one certain eidetic state as these areas are governed by one pure physical state. In contrast, regions with fast-changing physics quantities exhibit a multimode distribution across physics states, reflecting that these areas are influenced by a mixture of multiple states.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2 </span>Parallel Transolver++</h3>

<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To break the GPU memory bottleneck caused by feedforward layers of million-scale point representations, we design a highly optimized framework for PDE solving, which is based on the unique physics-learning design of Transolver.</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Parallelism formulation</h5>

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Through careful analysis, we observe that in addition to the point-wise feedforward layer, the computation of eidetic states within Physics-Attention can be efficiently distributed across multiple GPUs. Specifically, operations in Eq. (<a href="#S3.E1" title="Equation 1 ‣ 3 Revisiting Transolver ‣ Transolver++: An Accurate Neural Solver for PDEs on Million-Scale Geometries" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>), such as the weighted sum <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sum_{i=1}^{N}\mathbf{w}_{ij}\mathbf{x}_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>N</mi></msubsup><mrow><msub><mi>𝐰</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sum_{i=1}^{N}\mathbf{w}_{ij}\mathbf{x}_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> and the normalization denominator <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sum_{i=1}^{N}\mathbf{w}_{ij}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>N</mi></msubsup><msub><mi>𝐰</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sum_{i=1}^{N}\mathbf{w}_{ij}</annotation></semantics></math>, can be easily dispatched to multiple GPUs and calculated separately in parallel. Thus, we first separate the input mesh into multiple GPUs for parallel computing and only communicate when calculating attention among eidetic states.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Suppose that the initial separation splits input mesh into #gpu GPUs and the integral representation <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times C}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐱</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times C}</annotation></semantics></math> is split into <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{\mathbf{x}^{(1)},\cdots,\mathbf{x}^{(\#\text{gpu})}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msup><mi>𝐱</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋯</mo><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>𝐱</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>#</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mtext>gpu</mtext></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{\mathbf{x}^{(1)},\cdots,\mathbf{x}^{(\#\text{gpu})}\}</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{x}^{(k)}\in\mathbb{R}^{N_{k}\times C}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>𝐱</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{x}^{(k)}\in\mathbb{R}^{N_{k}\times C}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N_{k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N_{k}</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the number of mesh points dispatched to the <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math>-th GPU. Correspondingly, the point-wise slice weights <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{w}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times M}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐰</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{w}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times M}</annotation></semantics></math> is also separated into #gpu components <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{\mathbf{w}^{(1)},\cdots,\mathbf{w}^{(\#\text{gpu})}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msup><mi>𝐰</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋯</mo><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>𝐰</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>#</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mtext>gpu</mtext></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{\mathbf{w}^{(1)},\cdots,\mathbf{w}^{(\#\text{gpu})}\}</annotation></semantics></math> with <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{w}^{(k)}\in\mathbb{R}^{N_{k}\times M}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>𝐰</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{w}^{(k)}\in\mathbb{R}^{N_{k}\times M}</annotation></semantics></math>.
For clarity, we treat both multi-node-multi-GPU and single-node-multi-GPU configurations as a unified case. The calculation of eidetic states <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{s}_{j}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐬</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{s}_{j}</annotation></semantics></math> in Eq. (<a href="#S3.E1" title="Equation 1 ‣ 3 Revisiting Transolver ‣ Transolver++: An Accurate Neural Solver for PDEs on Million-Scale Geometries" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>) can be equivalently rewritten into the following parallelism formalization:</p>
<table id="S4.E5" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">

rspace="0.055em">⊕</mo><mrow><msubsup><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mrow><mi>#</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mtext>gpu</mtext></mrow></msub></msubsup><msubsup><mi>𝐰</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow><mrow><mo <td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(5)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\oplus" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>⊕</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\oplus</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the AllReduce operation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Patarasuk &amp; Yuan, 2009</a>)</cite>, which aggregates the results from all processes. In practice, the <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math>-th GPU first independently computes its partial sums for the numerator <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\sum_{i=1}^{N_{k}}\mathbf{w}_{ij}^{(k)}\mathbf{x}_{i}^{(k)})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msubsup><mo lspace="0em">∑</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></msubsup><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝐰</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>i</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\sum_{i=1}^{N_{k}}\mathbf{w}_{ij}^{(k)}\mathbf{x}_{i}^{(k)})</annotation></semantics></math> and denominator <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\sum_{i=1}^{N_{k}}\mathbf{w}_{ij}^{(k)})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msubsup><mo lspace="0em">∑</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></msubsup><msubsup><mi>𝐰</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\sum_{i=1}^{N_{k}}\mathbf{w}_{ij}^{(k)})</annotation></semantics></math> of <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N_{k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N_{k}</annotation></semantics></math> points. Next, these partial results are synchronized across GPUs to compute the eidetic states <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{s}_{j}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐬</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{s}_{j}</annotation></semantics></math>, highlighted by <span id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#0000FF;">blue</span>-marked steps in Algorithm <a href="#alg1" title="Algorithm 1 ‣ Overhead analysis ‣ 4.2 Parallel Transolver++ ‣ 4 Transolver++ ‣ Transolver++: An Accurate Neural Solver for PDEs on Million-Scale Geometries" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Overhead analysis</h5>

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Consider the input <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times C}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐱</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times C}</annotation></semantics></math> with <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>N</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N</annotation></semantics></math> mesh points and <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>C</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C</annotation></semantics></math> channels. To handle large model parameters in linear layers, tensor parallelism partitions the model parameters along the channel dimension. It reduces the memory consumption linearly but introduces an increase in communication overhead of <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O(N)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>N</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">O(N)</annotation></semantics></math>. Attention-optimized methods like RingAttention leverage the FlashAttention concept to distribute the outer loop using a ring topology, which results in <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O(N^{2})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>N</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">O(N^{2})</annotation></semantics></math> communication complexity, while DeepSpeed-Ulysses, similar to tensor parallelism, partitions the data along feature dimensions and yields an <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O(N)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>N</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">O(N)</annotation></semantics></math> communication volume. However, all of the above methods are not feasible when handling million-scale meshes as the communication overhead shown in Figure <a href="#S4.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 4.1 Physics-Attention with Eidetic States ‣ 4 Transolver++ ‣ Transolver++: An Accurate Neural Solver for PDEs on Million-Scale Geometries" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>(b) is unacceptable.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">In parallel Transolver++, each GPU computes two partial sums of size <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{O}(MC)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{O}(MC)</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{O}(M)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>M</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{O}(M)</annotation></semantics></math> separately, which are then synchronized across GPUs and cause a total communication volume of <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{O}(\#\text{gpu}\times M(C+1))" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>#</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mtext>gpu</mtext></mrow><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{O}(\#\text{gpu}\times M(C+1))</annotation></semantics></math>, invariant to input size.</p>
</div>
<figure id="alg1" class="ltx_figure ltx_float_algorithm ltx_framed ltx_framed_top">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="alg1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Algorithm 1</span> </span> Parallel Physics-Attention with Eidetic States</figcaption>
<div id="alg1.4" class="ltx_listing ltx_framed ltx_framed_topbottom ltx_listing">
<div id="alg1.l1" class="ltx_listingline">

</div>
<div id="alg1.l2" class="ltx_listingline">
                
                
               <span id="alg1.l2.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Output:</span> Updated output features <math id="alg1.l2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{x}^{\prime(k)}\in\mathbb{R}^{N_{k}\times C}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>𝐱</mi><mrow><mo rspace="0em">′</mo><mphantom></mphantom><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></msup><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{x}^{\prime(k)}\in\mathbb{R}^{N_{k}\times C}</annotation></semantics></math>.

               <span id="alg1.l3.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#808080;">// drop <math id="alg1.l3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{f}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#808080;" mathcolor="#808080">𝐟</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{f}</annotation></semantics></math> to save 50% memory.</span>

</div>
<div id="alg1.l4" class="ltx_listingline">
                
                
               Compute <math id="alg1.l4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}\cancel{\mathbf{f}^{(k)}}},\mathbf{x}^{(k)}\leftarrow\text{Project}(\mathbf{x}^{(k)})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><menclose style="--ltx-fg-color:#808080;" mathcolor="#808080" notation="updiagonalstrike"><mstyle style="--ltx-fg-color:#808080;" mathcolor="#808080"><msup><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#808080;" mathcolor="#808080">𝐟</mi><mrow><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#808080;" mathcolor="#808080" stretchy="false">(</mo><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#808080;" mathcolor="#808080">k</mi><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#808080;" mathcolor="#808080" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></mstyle></menclose><mo>,</mo><mrow><msup><mi>𝐱</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">←</mo><mrow><mtext>Project</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>𝐱</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}\cancel{\mathbf{f}^{(k)}}},\mathbf{x}^{(k)}\leftarrow\text{Project}(\mathbf{x}^{(k)})</annotation></semantics></math>

</div>
<div id="alg1.l5" class="ltx_listingline">
                
                
               Compute <math id="alg1.l5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{\tau}^{(k)}\leftarrow\tau_{0}+{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\text{Ada-Temp}(\mathbf{x}^{(k)})}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>τ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">←</mo><mrow><msub><mi>τ</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><mrow><mtext style="--ltx-fg-color:#0000FF;" mathcolor="#0000FF">Ada-Temp</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#0000FF;" mathcolor="#0000FF" stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#0000FF;" mathcolor="#0000FF">𝐱</mi><mrow><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#0000FF;" mathcolor="#0000FF" stretchy="false">(</mo><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#0000FF;" mathcolor="#0000FF">k</mi><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#0000FF;" mathcolor="#0000FF" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#0000FF;" mathcolor="#0000FF" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{\tau}^{(k)}\leftarrow\tau_{0}+{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\text{Ada-Temp}(\mathbf{x}^{(k)})}</annotation></semantics></math>

</div>
<div id="alg1.l6" class="ltx_listingline">
                
                
               Compute weights <math id="alg1.l6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{w}^{(k)}\leftarrow{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\text{Rep-Slice}(\mathbf{x}^{(k)},\mathbf{\tau}^{(k)})}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>𝐰</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">←</mo><mrow><mtext style="--ltx-fg-color:#0000FF;" mathcolor="#0000FF">Rep-Slice</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#0000FF;" mathcolor="#0000FF" stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#0000FF;" mathcolor="#0000FF">𝐱</mi><mrow><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#0000FF;" mathcolor="#0000FF" stretchy="false">(</mo><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#0000FF;" mathcolor="#0000FF">k</mi><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#0000FF;" mathcolor="#0000FF" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#0000FF;" mathcolor="#0000FF">τ</mi><mrow><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#0000FF;" mathcolor="#0000FF" stretchy="false">(</mo><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#0000FF;" mathcolor="#0000FF">k</mi><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#0000FF;" mathcolor="#0000FF" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#0000FF;" mathcolor="#0000FF" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{w}^{(k)}\leftarrow{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\text{Rep-Slice}(\mathbf{x}^{(k)},\mathbf{\tau}^{(k)})}</annotation></semantics></math>

</div>

</div>

</div>
<div id="alg1.l9" class="ltx_listingline">
                
                
               Compute eidetic states <math id="alg1.l9.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{s}^{(k)}\leftarrow\frac{\mathbf{w}^{(k)\sf T}{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\mathbf{x}^{(k)}}{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}\cancel{\mathbf{f}^{(k)}}}}{\mathbf{w}_{\text{norm}}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>𝐬</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">←</mo><mfrac><mrow><msup><mi>𝐰</mi><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝖳</mi></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#0000FF;" mathcolor="#0000FF">𝐱</mi><mrow><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#0000FF;" mathcolor="#0000FF" stretchy="false">(</mo><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#0000FF;" mathcolor="#0000FF">k</mi><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#0000FF;" mathcolor="#0000FF" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><menclose style="--ltx-fg-color:#808080;" mathcolor="#808080" notation="updiagonalstrike"><mstyle style="--ltx-fg-color:#808080;" mathcolor="#808080"><msup><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#808080;" mathcolor="#808080">𝐟</mi><mrow><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#808080;" mathcolor="#808080" stretchy="false">(</mo><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#808080;" mathcolor="#808080">k</mi><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#808080;" mathcolor="#808080" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></mstyle></menclose></mrow><msub><mi>𝐰</mi><mtext>norm</mtext></msub></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{s}^{(k)}\leftarrow\frac{\mathbf{w}^{(k)\sf T}{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\mathbf{x}^{(k)}}{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}\cancel{\mathbf{f}^{(k)}}}}{\mathbf{w}_{\text{norm}}}</annotation></semantics></math>

</div>
<div id="alg1.l10" class="ltx_listingline">
                
                
               <span id="alg1.l10.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#0000FF;"> Reduce eidetic states <math id="alg1.l10.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{s}\leftarrow\text{AllReduce}(\mathbf{s}^{(k)})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#0000FF;" mathcolor="#0000FF">𝐬</mi><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#0000FF;" mathcolor="#0000FF" stretchy="false">←</mo><mrow><mtext style="--ltx-fg-color:#0000FF;" mathcolor="#0000FF">AllReduce</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#0000FF;" mathcolor="#0000FF" stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#0000FF;" mathcolor="#0000FF">𝐬</mi><mrow><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#0000FF;" mathcolor="#0000FF" stretchy="false">(</mo><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#0000FF;" mathcolor="#0000FF">k</mi><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#0000FF;" mathcolor="#0000FF" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#0000FF;" mathcolor="#0000FF" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{s}\leftarrow\text{AllReduce}(\mathbf{s}^{(k)})</annotation></semantics></math></span>  <math id="alg1.l10.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{O}(MC)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#808080;" class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic" mathcolor="#808080" mathsize="0.700em">𝒪</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#808080;" mathcolor="#808080" maxsize="0.700em" minsize="0.700em">(</mo><mrow><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#808080;" mathcolor="#808080" mathsize="0.700em">M</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#808080;" mathcolor="#808080" mathsize="0.700em">C</mi></mrow><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#808080;" mathcolor="#808080" maxsize="0.700em" minsize="0.700em">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{O}(MC)</annotation></semantics></math>

<p id="S4.F4.2" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center ltx_align_center"><span id="S4.F4.2.1" class="ltx_text"><img src="2502.02414v1/standard.png" id="S4.F4.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/130;" width="476" height="130" alt="Refer to caption"></span></p>

</section>
<section id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Further speedup</h5>

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Also, we found that Transolver’s code implementation is somewhat over-parameterized. Specifically, Transolver projects the data onto both <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{x}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐱</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{x}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{f}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐟</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{f}</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{x}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐱</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{x}</annotation></semantics></math> is used to generate slice weights, and <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{f}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐟</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{f}</annotation></semantics></math> is combined with weights to generate physical states. This repetitive design brings double memory costs. In this paper, we find that eliminating <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{f}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐟</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{f}</annotation></semantics></math> (marked <span id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#808080;">gray</span> in Algorithm <a href="#alg1" title="Algorithm 1 ‣ Overhead analysis ‣ 4.2 Parallel Transolver++ ‣ 4 Transolver++ ‣ Transolver++: An Accurate Neural Solver for PDEs on Million-Scale Geometries" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>) can simply and successfully increase the single-GPU input point capacity to 1.2 million, without sacrificing the model’s performance.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Experiments</h2>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We extensively evaluate Transolver++ on six standard benchmarks and two industrial-level datasets with million-scale meshes, covering both physics and design-oriented metrics.</p>
</div>
<section id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Benchmarks</h5>

<div id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">As summarized in Table <a href="#S5.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ Benchmarks ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Transolver++: An Accurate Neural Solver for PDEs on Million-Scale Geometries" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, our experiments include both standard benchmarks and industrial simulations, which cover a broad range of mesh sizes. Specifically, the standard benchmarks include Elasticity, Plasticity, Airfoil, Pipe, NS2d, and Darcy, which are widely used in previous studies <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wu et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. To further evaluate the model’s efficacy in real applications, we also perform experiments on industrial design tasks, where we utilized DrivAerNet++ <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Elrefaie et al., 2024</a>)</cite> for car design and a newly simulated AirCraft dataset for 3D aircraft design. In addition to the error of predicted physics fields, we also measure the model performance for design by calculating drag and lift coefficients from predicted physics fields.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.T1" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 1: </span>Summary of experimental datasets, where #Mesh denotes the size of mesh points in each sample.</figcaption>

<td id="S5.T1.2.5.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_r" style="padding-left:4.0pt;padding-right:4.0pt;"><span id="S5.T1.2.5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps" style="font-size:90%;">Benchmarks</span></td>
