</figure>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Baselines</h5>

<div id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We widely compare Transolver++ against more than 20 advanced baselines, covering various types of approaches. These baselines include 12 neural operators, such as Galerkin <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citeyearpar">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">2021</a>)</cite>, LNO <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citeyearpar">(<a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">2024</a>)</cite>, and GINO <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citeyearpar">(<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">2023a</a>)</cite>, some of which are specifically designed for irregular meshes; 4 Transformer-based PDE solvers, including OFormer <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citeyearpar">(<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">2023c</a>)</cite>, FactFormer <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citeyearpar">(<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">2023d</a>)</cite>, GNOT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citeyearpar">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">2023</a>)</cite>, and Transolver <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citeyearpar">(<a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">2024</a>)</cite>; and 4 graph-neural-network-based methods: GraphSAGE <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citeyearpar">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">2017</a>)</cite>, PointNet <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citeyearpar">(<a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">2017</a>)</cite>, Graph U-Net <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citeyearpar">(<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">2019</a>)</cite>, and MeshGraphNet <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citeyearpar">(<a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">2021</a>)</cite>. Transolver is the previous state-of-the-art model. During experiments, we found that some neural operators designed for grids perform poorly for large-scale irregular meshes. Therefore, we only report their performance on standard benchmark datasets.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.1 </span>Standard Benchmarks</h3>

<section id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Setups</h5>

<div id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">As shown in Figure <a href="#S4.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ Overhead analysis ‣ 4.2 Parallel Transolver++ ‣ 4 Transolver++ ‣ Transolver++: An Accurate Neural Solver for PDEs on Million-Scale Geometries" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>(a), we compare the latest state-of-the-art neural PDE solvers with Transolver++ on six standard datasets covering a wide range of physics scenarios. For a fair comparison, we keep all model parameters within a fixed range. Specifically, in Transolver++, we set the model’s depth as eight layers, and the feature dimension is 128 or 256, depending on the scale of the data. The number of slices is chosen from {32, 64} to trade-off between computational cost and model performance.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Results</h5>

<div id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">As presented in Figure <a href="#S4.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ Overhead analysis ‣ 4.2 Parallel Transolver++ ‣ 4 Transolver++ ‣ Transolver++: An Accurate Neural Solver for PDEs on Million-Scale Geometries" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>(b), Transolver++ yields over 13% improvement w.r.t. the dataset-specific second-best baseline averaged from all six standard benchmarks, showing the efficacy of our proposed methods in handling complex geometries. To highlight the comparison, we only present top-3 baselines and Transolver++ in Figure <a href="#S4.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ Overhead analysis ‣ 4.2 Parallel Transolver++ ‣ 4 Transolver++ ‣ Transolver++: An Accurate Neural Solver for PDEs on Million-Scale Geometries" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>, which are chosen based on the overall performance. Full results for other baselines are provided in Table <a href="#A1.T5" title="Table 5 ‣ Appendix A Full Results on Standard Benchmarks ‣ Transolver++: An Accurate Neural Solver for PDEs on Million-Scale Geometries" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> of the Appendix.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">It is worth noticing that Transolver and Transolver++ significantly outperform other models in Elasticity, whose geometry is recorded as an unstructured point cloud. Going beyond Transolver, Transolver++ further boosts performance by learning eidetic physical states. As shown in Figure <a href="#S3.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 3 Revisiting Transolver ‣ Transolver++: An Accurate Neural Solver for PDEs on Million-Scale Geometries" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>, Transolver++ can learn more diverse slice partitioning, thereby enabling more accurate physics learning. More analyses on learned physical states can also be found in Appendix <a href="#A3" title="Appendix C More Visualizations ‣ Transolver++: An Accurate Neural Solver for PDEs on Million-Scale Geometries" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.T2" class="ltx_table">

<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 2: </span>Comparison on large geometries benchmarks. <ul id="S5.I1" class="ltx_itemize ltx_figure_panel">
<li id="S5.I1.ix1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item"></span>
<div id="S5.I1.ix1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.I1.ix1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><math id="S5.I1.ix1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ast" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo mathsize="0.800em">∗</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ast</annotation></semantics></math><span id="S5.I1.ix1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;"> These models cannot directly handle million-scale meshes as the model input. Thus, to enable comparison, we split the input mesh of these models into several pieces, independently infer them, and concatenate separately inferred outputs as their final results.</span></p>
</div></li>

</section>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.2 </span>PDEs on Large Geometries</h3>

<section id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Setups</h5>

<div id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To evaluate the performance in practical applications, we conduct experiments on two industrial datasets with million-scale meshes: DrivAerNet++ <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Elrefaie et al., 2024</a>)</cite> and Aircraft. The latter is newly presented by us, which is of high quality and simulated by aerodynamicists. To fully evaluate the model performance under different scales, we split DrivAerNet++ into two scales, one only with surface pressure (<math id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∼</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim</annotation></semantics></math>700k mesh points in each sample) and the other with full physics fields (2.5M mesh points).</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.F5" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2502.02414v1/datasets.png" id="S5.F5.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/226;" width="476" height="226" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 5: </span>Car and aircraft design to predict drag and lift coefficient under extremely complex geometries with million-scale meshes.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Results</h5>

<div id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#S5.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ Results ‣ 5.1 Standard Benchmarks ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Transolver++: An Accurate Neural Solver for PDEs on Million-Scale Geometries" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> demonstrates that Transolver++ achieved consistent state-of-the-art in all datasets with an average promotion of over 20%. In DrivAerNet++, our model is capable of handling 2.5 million meshes within 4 A100 GPUs and surpassing all other models by relative promotion of 11.0% and 12.6% on volume and surface field separately. In the surface field, our model still shows a prominent lead of 24.1% in DrivAerNet++ Surface and 30.4% in AirCraft.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We also observe that GNNs often degenerate quickly when handling large-scale meshes due to their geometric instability <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Klabunde &amp; Lemmerich, 2023</a>)</cite>. Additionally, Geo-FNO also performs poorly across nearly all datasets, as it attempts to map irregular meshes to uniform latent grids, a task that becomes especially difficult when the number of meshes scales up. These failures of our baselines further highlight the challenge of physics learning on million-scale geometries, while Transolver++ provides a practical solution, advancing an essential step to industrial applications.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">As shown in Figure <a href="#S5.F6" title="Figure 6 ‣ Results ‣ 5.2 PDEs on Large Geometries ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Transolver++: An Accurate Neural Solver for PDEs on Million-Scale Geometries" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>(b), our model has a lower relative error in most cases and excels in capturing the intrinsic physics variations in those regions with drastic changes, while other models tend to generate an over-smooth prediction, validating the effectiveness of learning eidetic states.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.T3" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 3: </span>Ablations on AirCraft. Relative L2 and <math id="S5.T3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>R</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> of lift coefficient are both recorded. <em id="S5.T3.5" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Ada-Temp</em> refers to Eq. (<a href="#S4.E3" title="Equation 3 ‣ Local adaptive mechanism ‣ 4.1 Physics-Attention with Eidetic States ‣ 4 Transolver++ ‣ Transolver++: An Accurate Neural Solver for PDEs on Million-Scale Geometries" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>), <em id="S5.T3.6" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Reparameter</em> is for Eq. (<a href="#S4.E4" title="Equation 4 ‣ Slice reparameterization ‣ 4.1 Physics-Attention with Eidetic States ‣ 4 Transolver++ ‣ Transolver++: An Accurate Neural Solver for PDEs on Million-Scale Geometries" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>) and <em id="S5.T3.7" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Speedup</em> represents removing <math id="S5.T3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{f}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐟</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{f}</annotation></semantics></math> in Algorithm <a href="#alg1" title="Algorithm 1 ‣ Overhead analysis ‣ 4.2 Parallel Transolver++ ‣ 4 Transolver++ ‣ Transolver++: An Accurate Neural Solver for PDEs on Million-Scale Geometries" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>.</figcaption>
<table id="S5.T3.8" class="ltx_tabular ltx_centering ltx_guessed_headers ltx_align_middle">
<thead class="ltx_thead">
<tr id="S5.T3.8.1" class="ltx_tr">
<th id="S5.T3.8.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_th_row ltx_border_r ltx_border_tt" rowspan="2"><span id="S5.T3.8.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps" style="font-size:90%;">Method</span></th>
<th id="S5.T3.8.1.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_border_tt" colspan="3"><span id="S5.T3.8.1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps" style="font-size:90%;">AirCraft</span></th></tr>
<tr id="S5.T3.8.2" class="ltx_tr">
<th id="S5.T3.8.2.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_th ltx_th_column"><math id="S5.T3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C_{L}\downarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi mathsize="0.900em">C</mi><mi mathsize="0.900em">L</mi></msub><mo mathsize="0.900em" stretchy="false">↓</mo><mphantom></mphantom></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C_{L}\downarrow</annotation></semantics></math></th>

<section id="S5.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.3 </span>Model Analysis</h3>

<div id="S5.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In addition to model comparisons, we also conduct a series of analysis experiments to provide an in-depth understanding of our model and the necessity of large geometries.</p>
</div>
<section id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Ablations</h5>

<div id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We conducted elaborative ablations on every component of Transolver++. As shown in Table <a href="#S5.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ Results ‣ 5.2 PDEs on Large Geometries ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Transolver++: An Accurate Neural Solver for PDEs on Million-Scale Geometries" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>, introducing the local adaptive mechanism significantly improves performance, which validates our motivation to learn eidetic states. With speed-up optimization and reparameterization techniques, the model achieves its best performance, fully demonstrating the effectiveness of our proposed design.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.T4" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 4: </span>KL-divergence between learned slice weights and uniform distribution in different layers on Elasticity. We choose {1, 3, 5, 7} layers and a higher value means a more diverse distribution.</figcaption>

</section>
<section id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Slice Analysis</h5>

<div id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">As shown in Figure <a href="#S5.F6" title="Figure 6 ‣ Results ‣ 5.2 PDEs on Large Geometries ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Transolver++: An Accurate Neural Solver for PDEs on Million-Scale Geometries" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>(a), Transolver++ can extract more diverse physical states than Transolver in million-scale meshes, enabling fine modeling for complex physics fields of driving cars. More visualization can be found in Appendix <a href="#A3" title="Appendix C More Visualizations ‣ Transolver++: An Accurate Neural Solver for PDEs on Million-Scale Geometries" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C</span></a>. Moreover, in Table <a href="#S5.T4" title="Table 4 ‣ Ablations ‣ 5.3 Model Analysis ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Transolver++: An Accurate Neural Solver for PDEs on Million-Scale Geometries" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>, we also calculate the KL divergence between learned slice weights and uniform distribution in different layers. These statistical results further demonstrate that Transolver++ can learn more diverse and varying slice distribution across all the layers.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Efficiency analysis</h5>

<div id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In addition to GPU memory (Figure <a href="#S1.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Transolver++: An Accurate Neural Solver for PDEs on Million-Scale Geometries" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>), we also measured the running time of different models on DrivAerNet++ datasets in Figure <a href="#S5.F6" title="Figure 6 ‣ Results ‣ 5.2 PDEs on Large Geometries ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Transolver++: An Accurate Neural Solver for PDEs on Million-Scale Geometries" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> (c.1). To ensure a fair comparison, all models’ parameter sizes are well aligned in our experiments and we only compare Transolver++ with Transformer-based methods here, since GNNs struggle to handle million-scale meshes. We can find that Transolver++ strikes a favorable balance between performance and efficiency, outperforming most models in terms of speed. Moreover, at the same size of input mesh points, our method exhibits the lowest memory usage, highlighting its efficiency in handling large-scale data without sacrificing accuracy.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Why we need large geometries</h5>

<div id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">From the car mesh comparison in Figure <a href="#S1.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Transolver++: An Accurate Neural Solver for PDEs on Million-Scale Geometries" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>(b), we can observe that large geometries differ significantly from smaller-scale ones in terms of details, which directly affects the accuracy of the simulation. While previous models <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2021</a>)</cite> claim to be resolution-invariant and aim to apply directly to large-scale geometries, our experiments in Figure <a href="#S5.F6" title="Figure 6 ‣ Results ‣ 5.2 PDEs on Large Geometries ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Transolver++: An Accurate Neural Solver for PDEs on Million-Scale Geometries" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> (c.2) show that without training on large meshes, the model will fall short in the fine-grained physics modeling, resulting in an insufficient and limited performance, which further necessitates the capability of handling larger geometries.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.F7" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2502.02414v1/scalability.svg" id="S5.F7.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/210;" width="476" height="210"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 7: </span>Evaluation of the model scalability in terms of data size and parameter size. Our default setting is 150 cases and 4 layers.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px5" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Scalability</h5>

<div id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate the scalability of Transolver++ across different numbers of training samples and model parameters of different sizes by altering the number of layers. From Figure <a href="#S5.F7" title="Figure 7 ‣ Why we need large geometries ‣ 5.3 Model Analysis ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Transolver++: An Accurate Neural Solver for PDEs on Million-Scale Geometries" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>, we can find that our model can consistently benefit from large data and large models, revealing its potential to be the backbone of PDE-solving foundation models.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S6" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">6 </span>Conclusion</h2>

<div id="S6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In pursuit of practical neural solvers, this paper presents Transolver++, which enables the first success in accurately solving PDEs discretized on million-scale geometries. Specifically, we upgrade the vanilla Transolver by introducing eidetic states and a highly optimized parallel framework, empowering Transolver++ with better physics learning and computation efficiency. As a result, our model achieves significant advancement in industrial design tasks, demonstrating favorable efficiency and scalability, which can serve as a neat backbone of PDE-solving foundation models.</p>
</div>
</section>

<section id="A1" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix A </span>Full Results on Standard Benchmarks</h2>

<div id="A1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Due to the space limitation of the main text, we present the full results of model performance on standard benchmarks here, as a supplement to Figure <a href="#S4.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ Overhead analysis ‣ 4.2 Parallel Transolver++ ‣ 4 Transolver++ ‣ Transolver++: An Accurate Neural Solver for PDEs on Million-Scale Geometries" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>. As shown in Table <a href="#A1.T5" title="Table 5 ‣ Appendix A Full Results on Standard Benchmarks ‣ Transolver++: An Accurate Neural Solver for PDEs on Million-Scale Geometries" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>, Transolver++ demonstrates superior performance across six standard PDE benchmarks, achieving the lowest relative L2 error in all PDE-solving tasks with an averaged relative promotion of 13%.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">For models marked with an asterisk (*), we carefully reproduced the results by running the models more than three times and enabled fair and reliable comparison by maintaining the model parameter counts within a closely comparable range with other models. Specifically, we adjust LNO and reduce its default dimension from 256 to 192 in elasticity, as its parameter count is already three times larger than the other largest models. As discussed in previous studies <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wu et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, Transformer-based models usually benefit from large parameter sizes. This approach minimizes the potential influence of parameter variations and highlights the performance improvements achieved by our method under similar computation costs.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A1.T5" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 5: </span>Model performance on six standard PDE benchmarks is evaluated using the relative L2 error. The result marked with an asterisk (*) indicates a reproduced outcome, where the parameter counts and configurations of the baseline methods are carefully aligned to ensure a fair comparison. “/” means that the baseline cannot apply to this benchmark.</figcaption>

<section id="A2" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix B </span>Implementation Details</h2>

<div id="A2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this section, we provide detailed descriptions of the benchmarks, baseline methods, and implementation setups to ensure reproducibility and facilitate comparisons.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A2.T6" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 6: </span>Details of different benchmarks, including geometric type, number of mesh points, as well as the type of input and output, etc. The split of the dataset is also provided to ensure reproducibility, which is listed in the order of (training samples, test samples).</figcaption>
<table id="A2.T6.2" class="ltx_tabular ltx_align_middle">
<tbody class="ltx_tbody">
<tr id="A2.T6.2.1" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="A2.T6.2.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_r ltx_border_tt" style="padding-left:5.5pt;padding-right:5.5pt;"><span id="A2.T6.2.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps" style="font-size:90%;">Type</span></td>
<td id="A2.T6.2.1.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_r ltx_border_tt" style="padding-left:5.5pt;padding-right:5.5pt;"><span id="A2.T6.2.1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps" style="font-size:90%;">Benchmark</span></td>
<td id="A2.T6.2.1.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_r ltx_border_tt" style="padding-left:5.5pt;padding-right:5.5pt;"><span id="A2.T6.2.1.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps" style="font-size:90%;">#Dim</span></td>
<td id="A2.T6.2.1.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_r ltx_border_tt" style="padding-left:5.5pt;padding-right:5.5pt;"><span id="A2.T6.2.1.4.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps" style="font-size:90%;">#Meshes</span></td>
<td id="A2.T6.2.1.5" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_r ltx_border_tt" style="padding-left:5.5pt;padding-right:5.5pt;"><span id="A2.T6.2.1.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps" style="font-size:90%;">#Input</span></td>

<section id="A2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.1 </span>Benchmarks</h3>

<div id="A2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate our method on six standard PDE benchmarks, including Elasticity, Plasticity, Airfoil, Pipe, NS2D, and Darcy, as well as two industrial datasets, DrivAerNet++ and AirCraft. These benchmarks cover a wide range of physics simulation tasks, varying in complexity and geometry, and serve as a comprehensive benchmarks for assessing the effectiveness of neural PDE solvers as shown in Table <a href="#A2.T6" title="Table 6 ‣ Appendix B Implementation Details ‣ Transolver++: An Accurate Neural Solver for PDEs on Million-Scale Geometries" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>. Here are the details of these datasets.</p>
</div>
<section id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Elasticity</h5>

<div id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This benchmark is generated by the simulations of the stress field in a hyper-elastic solid body under tension, which is governed by a stress-strain relationship using the Rivlin-Saunders material model <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2022</a>)</cite>. Each case involves a unit cell of 972 points with a void in the middle , clamped at the bottom edge and subjected to tension on the top. Elasticity contains a total of 1200 samples, with 1000 for training and 200 for testing.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Plasticity</h5>

<div id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This benchmark is generated by the simulation of a plastic forging problem, where a block is impacted by a frictionless die moving at a constant speed <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2022</a>)</cite>. An elastoplastic constitutive model is adopted to model this physical system with 900 training and 80 testing samples. The input is the external force on every mesh with the shape of 101 <math id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> 31, and the output is the time-dependent deformation and mesh grid over 20 timesteps.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Airfoil</h5>

<div id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This benchmark is generated from simulations of transonic flow over an airfoil, governed by Euler’s equations <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2022</a>)</cite>. The whole field is discretized to unstructured meshes in the shape of 221 <math id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> 51 as the input and the output is the corresponding Mach number on these meshes. The dataset includes 1000 training samples and 200 test samples that are based on the initial NACA-0012 shape.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Pipe</h5>

<div id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This benchmark consists of simulations of incompressible flow in a pipe, governed by the Navier-Stokes equation with viscosity <math id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\nu=0.005" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ν</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.005</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\nu=0.005</annotation></semantics></math> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2022</a>)</cite>. The pipe has a length of 10 and a width of 1, with its centerline parameterized by cubic polynomials determined by five control nodes. The dataset also contains 1000 training and 200 testing samples, whose inputs are the mesh point locations 129 <math id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> 129 and outputs are the horizontal velocity field.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px5" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Navier-Stokes</h5>

<div id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This benchmark consists of simulations of the 2D Navier-Stokes equations in vorticity form on the unit torus <math id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px5.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(0,1)^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(0,1)^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2021</a>)</cite>. The objective is, given the past velocity, to predict future velocity for 10 steps on discretized meshes in the shape of 64 <math id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px5.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> 64. The inputs are the velocity for the past 10 steps, while the outputs provide the future velocity for 10 timesteps. The dataset also includes 1000 samples for training and 200 for testing.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px6" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Darcy</h5>

<div id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This benchmark consists of simulations of the steady-state Darcy Flow in two dimensions, governed by a second-order elliptic equation on the unit square <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2022</a>)</cite>. The input is the structure of the porous medium and the output is the corresponding fluid pressure. The dataset contains 1000 training samples and 200 testing samples, generated using a second-order finite difference scheme on 421 <math id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px6.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> 421 uniform grids and later downsampled to <math id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px6.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="85\times 85" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>85</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>85</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">85\times 85</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px7" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">DrivAerNet++</h5>

<div id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px7.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px7.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This benchmark <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Elrefaie et al., 2024</a>)</cite> is a large and comprehensive dataset for aerodynamic car design, featuring high-fidelity computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations. It includes over 8,000 car designs with various configurations of wheel and underbody design. To ensure efficiency while maintaining diversity, we select 200 representative cases from these designs. Notably, in our experiments, DrivAerNet++ is then divided into two subsets with different levels of resolution. The first subset, as shown in Table <a href="#A2.T6" title="Table 6 ‣ Appendix B Implementation Details ‣ Transolver++: An Accurate Neural Solver for PDEs on Million-Scale Geometries" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>, only consists of surface meshes, where each mesh point is characterized by its 3D position <math id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px7.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(x,y,z)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(x,y,z)</annotation></semantics></math>, surface normal vector <math id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px7.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(u_{x},u_{y},u_{z})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>x</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>y</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>z</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(u_{x},u_{y},u_{z})</annotation></semantics></math>, and signed distance function (SDF). The output for this subset is the surface pressure on these meshes. The second subset provides a full 3D pressure and velocity field, significantly increasing the dataset’s complexity, with the number of mesh points reaching approximately 2.5 million and requiring the model to predict surface pressure, velocity and pressure of the surrounding area. The dataset consists of 190 training samples and 10 test samples, offering a rigorous benchmark for evaluating aerodynamic modeling at different levels of fidelity.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px8" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">AirCraft</h5>

<div id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px8.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px8.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This benchmark includes simulations of over 30 aircraft designs under 5 different incoming flow conditions, varying in Mach number, angle of attack, and sideslip angle. Unlike commonly used aerodynamics datasets such as Airfoil, the AirCraft dataset discretizes each aircraft into approximately 300,000 3D mesh points, offering a significantly higher resolution for capturing complex aerodynamic phenomena. Each mesh point is characterized by its spatial coordinates <math id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px8.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(x,y,z)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(x,y,z)</annotation></semantics></math> and surface normal vector, serving as the input. These high-fidelity computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations, conducted by aerodynamicists in an aircraft design institution, ensure precise and realistic aerodynamic modeling. The dataset requires predicting six key physical quantities: pressure coefficient <math id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px8.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C_{p}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C_{p}</annotation></semantics></math>, fluid density <math id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px8.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math>, velocity components (<math id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px8.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>u</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px8.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="v" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>v</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">v</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px8.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>w</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w</annotation></semantics></math>), and pressure <math id="A2.SS1.SSS0.Px8.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>p</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p</annotation></semantics></math>. With 140 training cases and 10 test cases, this dataset presents intricate aerodynamic interactions, making it a rigorous benchmark for assessing model scalability and accuracy.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.2 </span>Metrics</h3>

<div id="A2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To comprehensively evaluate model performance across different datasets and prediction tasks, we adopt relative L2 error as the primary evaluation metric. For large-scale datasets, we evaluate both field and coefficient predictions separately. And we further introduce R-squared (<math id="A2.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>R</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R^{2}</annotation></semantics></math>) score as an additional metric to assess the accuracy of coefficient predictions. In this section, we would explain how these metrics are applied to different dataset categories in detail.</p>
</div>
<section id="A2.SS2.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">B.2.1 </span>Standard Benchmarks</h4>

<div id="A2.SS2.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS2.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For standard benchmark datasets, model performance is assessed using the relative L2 error, which directly measures the difference between the predicted output and the ground truth. Given an output field <math id="A2.SS2.SSS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{y}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>y</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{y}</annotation></semantics></math> predicted by the model and the ground truth <math id="A2.SS2.SSS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>y</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y</annotation></semantics></math>, the relative L2 error is computed as:</p>
<table id="A2.E6" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A2.E6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{Relative L2}=\frac{\|\hat{\mathbf{y}}-\mathbf{y}\|_{2}}{\|\mathbf{y}\|_{2}}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mtext>Relative L2</mtext><mo>=</mo><mfrac><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐲</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>−</mo><mi>𝐲</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mi>𝐲</mi><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub></mfrac></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{Relative L2}=\frac{\|\hat{\mathbf{y}}-\mathbf{y}\|_{2}}{\|\mathbf{y}\|_{2}}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(6)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A2.SS2.SSS1.p1.2" class="ltx_p">This metric on standard benchmarks is reported in the Table <a href="#A1.T5" title="Table 5 ‣ Appendix A Full Results on Standard Benchmarks ‣ Transolver++: An Accurate Neural Solver for PDEs on Million-Scale Geometries" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>, providing a direct comparison across different models.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS2.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">B.2.2 </span>Large-Scale Datasets</h4>

<section id="A2.SS2.SSS2.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Field and Coefficient Errors</h5>

<div id="A2.SS2.SSS2.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS2.SSS2.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For large-scale datasets, we decompose the relative L2 error into two components to gain deeper insights into model performance. Since large-scale datasets often involve both surface and volume (refers to the surrounding area) data, we separately compute the relative L2 error for surface fields and volume fields. This distinction allows us to evaluate how well the model captures different types of physical information. In addition to predicting field values, some datasets require models to infer physical coefficients that characterize the feature of the system. The relative L2 error is also applied to these coefficients to measure prediction accuracy.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS2.SSS2.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS2.SSS2.Px1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">For example, in AirCraft, lift coefficient is calculated to measure the aerodynamic lift force on the body of an aircraft, which is a key metric to assess the lift performance of an aircraft under a certain flow condition. The lift coefficient is defined as:</p>
<table id="A2.E7" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A2.E7.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="C_{L}=\frac{1}{\frac{1}{2}\rho v_{\infty}^{2}A}\int_{S}\left(-p\mathbf{n}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{l}}+\boldsymbol{\tau}\mathbf{n}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{l}}\right){\rm d}S," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>L</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>ρ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>v</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>A</mi></mrow></mfrac><msub><mo rspace="0em">∫</mo><mi>S</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mo lspace="0em">−</mo><mi>p</mi><mi>𝐧</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐥</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>+</mo><mi>𝝉</mi><mi>𝐧</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐥</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>)</mo></mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>S</mi><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C_{L}=\frac{1}{\frac{1}{2}\rho v_{\infty}^{2}A}\int_{S}\left(-p\mathbf{n}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{l}}+\boldsymbol{\tau}\mathbf{n}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{l}}\right){\rm d}S,</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(7)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A2.SS2.SSS2.Px1.p2.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="A2.SS2.SSS2.Px1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>p</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p</annotation></semantics></math> is the pressure field on the surface, <math id="A2.SS2.SSS2.Px1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{n}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐧</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{n}</annotation></semantics></math> is the unit normal vector of the surface, <math id="A2.SS2.SSS2.Px1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{\mathbf{l}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐥</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\mathbf{l}}</annotation></semantics></math> is the unit vector in the lift direction, <math id="A2.SS2.SSS2.Px1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\boldsymbol{\tau}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝝉</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\boldsymbol{\tau}</annotation></semantics></math> is the shear stress tensor and <math id="A2.SS2.SSS2.Px1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>S</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S</annotation></semantics></math> is the surface of the aircraft.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS2.SSS2.Px1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS2.SSS2.Px1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Also in car design, drag coefficient is a crucial metric to quantify the aerodynamic drag force on the body of a vehicle, which can be used to improve fuel efficiency and the performance of vehicles. The drag coefficient is defined as:</p>
<table id="A2.E8" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A2.E8.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="C_{D}=\frac{1}{\frac{1}{2}\rho v_{\infty}^{2}A}\int_{S}\left(-p\mathbf{n}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{d}}+\boldsymbol{\tau}\mathbf{n}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{d}}\right){\rm d}S," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>D</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>ρ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>v</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>A</mi></mrow></mfrac><msub><mo rspace="0em">∫</mo><mi>S</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mo lspace="0em">−</mo><mi>p</mi><mi>𝐧</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐝</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>+</mo><mi>𝝉</mi><mi>𝐧</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐝</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>)</mo></mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>S</mi><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C_{D}=\frac{1}{\frac{1}{2}\rho v_{\infty}^{2}A}\int_{S}\left(-p\mathbf{n}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{d}}+\boldsymbol{\tau}\mathbf{n}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{d}}\right){\rm d}S,</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(8)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A2.SS2.SSS2.Px1.p3.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="A2.SS2.SSS2.Px1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>p</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p</annotation></semantics></math> is the surface pressure, <math id="A2.SS2.SSS2.Px1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{n}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐧</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{n}</annotation></semantics></math> is the unit normal vector of the surface, <math id="A2.SS2.SSS2.Px1.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{\mathbf{d}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐝</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\mathbf{d}}</annotation></semantics></math> is the unit vector in the drag direction, <math id="A2.SS2.SSS2.Px1.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\boldsymbol{\tau}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝝉</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\boldsymbol{\tau}</annotation></semantics></math> is the shear stress tensor and <math id="A2.SS2.SSS2.Px1.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>S</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S</annotation></semantics></math> is the surface of the vehicle.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS2.SSS2.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">R-squared Score for Coefficient Predictions</h5>

<div id="A2.SS2.SSS2.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS2.SSS2.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To further evaluate the model’s ability to predict physical coefficients, we introduce the R-squared (<math id="A2.SS2.SSS2.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>R</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R^{2}</annotation></semantics></math>) score as an additional metric. The <math id="A2.SS2.SSS2.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>R</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> score is computed as:</p>
<table id="A2.E9" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A2.E9.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R^{2}=1-\frac{\sum_{i}(y_{i}-\hat{y}_{i})^{2}}{\sum_{i}(y_{i}-\bar{y})^{2}}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>R</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mo>∑</mo><mi>i</mi></msub><msup><mrow><mo lspace="0em" stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>y</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mrow><msub><mo>∑</mo><mi>i</mi></msub><msup><mrow><mo lspace="0em" stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>y</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mfrac></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R^{2}=1-\frac{\sum_{i}(y_{i}-\hat{y}_{i})^{2}}{\sum_{i}(y_{i}-\bar{y})^{2}},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(9)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A2.SS2.SSS2.Px2.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="A2.SS2.SSS2.Px2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{y}_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>y</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{y}_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> is the <math id="A2.SS2.SSS2.Px2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math>-th of the predicted coefficients, <math id="A2.SS2.SSS2.Px2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> is the <math id="A2.SS2.SSS2.Px2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math>-th ground truth, and <math id="A2.SS2.SSS2.Px2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bar{y}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>y</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bar{y}</annotation></semantics></math> is the mean of the ground truth values. An <math id="A2.SS2.SSS2.Px2.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>R</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> score closer to 1 indicates better model performance, while lower values suggest less accurate predictions. This metric measures how well the model learns the physical quantitiy fields among all samples.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A2.T7" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 7: </span>Implementation details of Transolver++ including training and model configuration. Training configurations are identical to previous methods <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wu et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hao et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Deng et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Elrefaie et al., 2024</a>)</cite> and shared in all baselines. <math id="A2.T7.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{v}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mi>v</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{v}}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A2.T7.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{s}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{s}}</annotation></semantics></math> refer to the loss on volume (surrounding area) and surface physics fields respectively.</figcaption>

<td id="A2.T7.2.9.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb ltx_border_t" style="padding-left:2.0pt;padding-right:2.0pt;" rowspan="3"><span id="A2.T7.2.9.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps" style="font-size:90%;">200</span></td>

<td id="A2.T7.2.9.5" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_t" style="padding-left:2.0pt;padding-right:2.0pt;"><span id="A2.T7.2.9.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps" style="font-size:90%;">Adam</span></td>
<td id="A2.T7.2.9.6" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb ltx_border_r ltx_border_t" style="padding-left:2.0pt;padding-right:2.0pt;" rowspan="3"><span id="A2.T7.2.9.6.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps" style="font-size:90%;">1</span></td>
<td id="A2.T7.2.9.7" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb ltx_border_t" style="padding-left:2.0pt;padding-right:2.0pt;" rowspan="3"><span id="A2.T7.2.9.7.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps" style="font-size:90%;">4</span></td>
<td id="A2.T7.2.9.8" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb ltx_border_t" style="padding-left:2.0pt;padding-right:2.0pt;" rowspan="3"><span id="A2.T7.2.9.8.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps" style="font-size:90%;">8</span></td>
<td id="A2.T7.2.9.9" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb ltx_border_t" style="padding-left:2.0pt;padding-right:2.0pt;" rowspan="3"><span id="A2.T7.2.9.9.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps" style="font-size:90%;">256</span></td>
<td id="A2.T7.2.9.10" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb ltx_border_t" style="padding-left:2.0pt;padding-right:2.0pt;" rowspan="3"><span id="A2.T7.2.9.10.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps" style="font-size:90%;">32</span></td></tr>
<tr id="A2.T7.2.10" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="A2.T7.2.10.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_r" style="padding-left:2.0pt;padding-right:2.0pt;"><span id="A2.T7.2.10.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps" style="font-size:90%;">DrivAerNet++ Surf</span></td>
<td id="A2.T7.2.10.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center" style="padding-left:2.0pt;padding-right:2.0pt;"><math id="A2.T7.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{s}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic" mathsize="0.900em">ℒ</mi><mi mathsize="0.900em">s</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{s}}</annotation></semantics></math></td>

</figure>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.3 </span>Baselines and Implementations</h3>

<div id="A2.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We conduct extensive comparisons between Transolver++ and over 20 state-of-the-art baselines, encompassing a diverse range of methods for solving partial differential equations (PDEs). These baselines include typical neural operators, Transformer-based PDE solvers, and graph neural networks (GNNs) and are tested under the same training configurations as shown in Table <a href="#A2.T7" title="Table 7 ‣ R-squared Score for Coefficient Predictions ‣ B.2.2 Large-Scale Datasets ‣ B.2 Metrics ‣ Appendix B Implementation Details ‣ Transolver++: An Accurate Neural Solver for PDEs on Million-Scale Geometries" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>. To ensure a rigorous comparison, we obtain the open-source implementations of these models and carefully verify their consistency with the original papers before training.</p>
</div>
<section id="A2.SS3.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">B.3.1 </span>Standard Benchmarks</h4>

<div id="A2.SS3.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS3.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We try to be as loyal to the original settings of baselines as possible. However, when the model parameters count is too large to conduct a fair comparison, we would change either the number of blocks or the hidden dimension to ensure a fair comparison. As we mentioned before, Transformer-based models usually benefit from large parameter sizes <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wu et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. Thus, the alignment of parameter size is essential to control the variable and highlight the performance difference caused by architecture design. Here are detailed implementations.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS3.SSS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS3.SSS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Specifically, we adjust LNO and reduce its default dimension from 256 to 192 in elasticity, as its parameter count is already three times larger than the other largest models, while other models’ settings remain unchanged.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS3.SSS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS3.SSS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Besides, we carefully review the original papers of these baseline models to make sure that they are fully tuned on their hyper-parameters. For all the models whose data settings align exactly with ours, such as FNO <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2021</a>)</cite>, Geo-FNO <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2022</a>)</cite>, GNOT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hao et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, OFormer <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2023c</a>)</cite>, Transolver <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wu et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, we directly adopt the results reported in their respective publications. For other models, we refer to the results presented in LSM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wu et al., 2023</a>)</cite> and Transolver <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wu et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, as these works have conducted comprehensive and rigorous hyper-parameter tuning to ensure a fair and reliable comparison.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS3.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">B.3.2 </span>Industrial Applications</h4>

<div id="A2.SS3.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS3.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For DrivAerNet++ and AirCraft datasets, most of the baseline models are unable to handle million-scale meshes directly. To address this, we subsample the dataset to 50k meshes point and reconstruct the meshes using K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Peterson, 2009</a>)</cite> method to preserve essential geometric relationships.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS3.SSS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS3.SSS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Specifically during training, we apply a random subsampling strategy at the beginning of each epoch and reconstruct meshes for only once in each case to maintain consistency of the total step count compared to other baselines capable of handling million-scale meshes. For testing, we perform a complete subsampling operation, obtaining multiple partial predictions across different subsampled sets. These predictions are then aggregated and concatenated to reconstruct the full output for each test case. The relative L2 error is subsequently computed on the concatenated predictions, and the final results are reported in Table <a href="#S5.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ Results ‣ 5.1 Standard Benchmarks ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Transolver++: An Accurate Neural Solver for PDEs on Million-Scale Geometries" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>. Furthermore, lift and drag coefficient are also computed based on the reconstructed outputs following their respective formulations in Eq. (<a href="#A2.E8" title="Equation 8 ‣ Field and Coefficient Errors ‣ B.2.2 Large-Scale Datasets ‣ B.2 Metrics ‣ Appendix B Implementation Details ‣ Transolver++: An Accurate Neural Solver for PDEs on Million-Scale Geometries" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a>) and Eq. (<a href="#A2.E9" title="Equation 9 ‣ R-squared Score for Coefficient Predictions ‣ B.2.2 Large-Scale Datasets ‣ B.2 Metrics ‣ Appendix B Implementation Details ‣ Transolver++: An Accurate Neural Solver for PDEs on Million-Scale Geometries" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS3.SSS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS3.SSS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">In terms of model configurations, each model has been extensively tuned on their hyperparameters, especially graph neural networks (GNNs) for their extreme instability <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Klabunde &amp; Lemmerich, 2023</a>)</cite> when dealing with million-scale meshes. To minimize human bias, we employ a standardized tuning strategy by systematically changing the hidden dimension from {64, 128, 256, 512}, the number of layers from {2, 4, 6, 8, 10} along with tuning model-specific hyperparameters. During this process, we observe that almost all GNNs experienced geometric instability <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Morris et al., 2023</a>)</cite> when applied to the DrivAerNet++ Full dataset with approximately 2.5 million mesh points per case. Out of all baselines, Transolver achieves the second-best performance, benefiting from its Slice-Deslice mechanism, which improves its stability and scalability, while Transolver++ surpasses it by introducing eidetic physical states and a parallelism framework that can directly handle million-scale meshes with enhanced efficiency. In Transolver++, we set the number of slices to 32 and its channels to 256 with 4 layers of Transolver++ block to balance efficiency and performance. And we only need to adopt parallelism to Transolver++ for the DrivAerNet++ Full benchamrk on only 4 A100 GPUs at most.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A3" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix C </span>More Visualizations</h2>

<div id="A3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">As a supplement to Figure <a href="#S5.F6" title="Figure 6 ‣ Results ‣ 5.2 PDEs on Large Geometries ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Transolver++: An Accurate Neural Solver for PDEs on Million-Scale Geometries" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> of the main text, in this section, we will provide detailed visualization of the eidetic physical states of Transolver++ as well as case study showcases on different datasets.</p>
</div>
<section id="A3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">C.1 </span>Eidetic States Visualization</h3>

<div id="A3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Here, for simplicity and clarity, we present visualizations of the eidetic physical states on four representative benchmarks: DrivAerNet++ Surf, Airplane, Airfoil, and Elasticity. We further compare these states with those learned by Transolver, demonstrating the effectiveness of our approach in capturing eidetic states under complex physical geometries. All visualizations are extracted from the final layer of each model to provide a direct comparison of their learned representations.</p>
</div>

<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 8: </span>Visualizations of 32 physical or eidetic states learned in the final layer of models on DrivAetNet++ Surface. <section id="A3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">C.2 </span>Case Studies</h3>

<div id="A3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In addition to the Figure <a href="#S5.F6" title="Figure 6 ‣ Results ‣ 5.2 PDEs on Large Geometries ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Transolver++: An Accurate Neural Solver for PDEs on Million-Scale Geometries" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> in the main text, here we provide more showcase comparisons in Figure <a href="#A3.F14" title="Figure 14 ‣ C.2 Case Studies ‣ Appendix C More Visualizations ‣ Transolver++: An Accurate Neural Solver for PDEs on Million-Scale Geometries" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">14</span></a>, <a href="#A3.F15" title="Figure 15 ‣ C.2 Case Studies ‣ Appendix C More Visualizations ‣ Transolver++: An Accurate Neural Solver for PDEs on Million-Scale Geometries" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">15</span></a> and <a href="#A3.F16" title="Figure 16 ‣ C.2 Case Studies ‣ Appendix C More Visualizations ‣ Transolver++: An Accurate Neural Solver for PDEs on Million-Scale Geometries" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">16</span></a>. Specifically, we compare our model with the strong baselines in the respective datasets, where Transolver is selected for the comparison in standard benchmarks and both Transolver and GNOT are compared in industrial datasets.</p>
</div>
